runs.text: Long-run average cost shows the lowest attainable cost per unit when every input and plant size can vary. Scale can make specialized tasks and equipment economical, lowering LRAC over a range. Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary. Falling long-run average cost as output expands is economies of scale.

Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Interpret LRAC, Economies & Diseconomies of Scale.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Long-run average cost shows the lowest attainable cost per unit when every input and plant size can vary. Scale can make specialized tasks and equipment economical, lowering LRAC over a range. Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary. Falling long-run average cost as output expands is economies of scale.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary.
A learner reads a downward-sloping LRAC segment as diseconomies of scale.
The concepts apply to different horizons and input changes.
A very large firm becomes harder to coordinate.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse scale and diminishing returns. Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING LONG-RUN AVERAGE COST

The LRAC curve falls from about $20 at 30 units to its minimum of about $12 at 60 units, showing economies of scale. It then rises back toward $20 by 90 units, showing diseconomies of scale. The cost-minimizing scale is approximately 60 units.
